Let me just preface this post by saying that I primarily game on PC, and by no means do I believe consoles are better. But to say that they are obsolete is a bit of an overstatement. While they may not be more powerful, there is a reason someone might prefer consoles.

One of the main benefits consoles have is that every unit of a specific console, (e.g. all standard PS4s), uses the same hardware; whereas PCs can and will have a myriad of different builds. Even though the console hardware is not as strong, it allows developers to provide a more consistent experience for their userbase.

When a game developer is designing their game, it's much easier for them to optimize the game's performance if they know that every machine it runs on will have the same specs. This is because they can build the game for their own console, and be confident that their players will achieve (mostly) identical performance, due to the uniformity of hardware specs. It's a much more reliable approach than PC development, because even though running 2 x 1080ti's is lightyears faster than a console, some players might be running a single 1060, a 680, an AMD card, or maybe even integrated graphics.

They have to expend more effort factoring in this uncertainty to figure out what the limits of the game should be, as well as wasting time developing resources to adjust game settings on a per machine basis. Additionally, it restricts a lot of hacky hardware tricks that can help squeeze out every little bit of performance from a device.

Although this is assuming the devs aren't just outsourcing it to asia, or importing incompetent H1Bindis for cheap labor. Because then it's likely they just don't give a shit about performance.

"Temporal redundancy notes that successive frames in a video sequence are very similar. Typically a video would be in the order of 20-30 frames per second, and nothing much changes in 1/30 of a second. Take any DVD and pause it, then move it on one frame and note how similar the 2 images are. So, instead of encoding each frame independently, MPEG-4 (and other compression standards) only encode the difference between successive frames (using motion estimation to find the difference between frames)

Spatial redundancy takes advantage of the fact that in general the colour spread across images tends to be quite low frequency. By this I mean that neighbouring pixels tend to have similar colours. For example, in an image of you wearing a red jumper, all of the pixels that represent your jumper would have very similar colour. It is possible to use the DCT to transform the pixel values into the frequency space, where some high frequency information can be thrown away. Then, when the reverse DCT is performed (during decoding), the image is now without the thrown away high-frequency information."

In early March, U.S. District Court Judge Colleen McMahon ordered that all inmates at the nearby federal jail be screened for fevers, and said they should not appear in court if they have a temperature of 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit or higher.
